finding: Unstructured sparsity is not automatically memory-efficient.
evidence: At 0% and 25% sparsity, estimated total memory is worse than dense fp32 because each nonzero stores value plus index.
interpretation: Sparsity needs high zero density or efficient sparse formats to become useful.

finding: 50% sparsity is the break-even point in the current unstructured sparse fp32 model.
evidence: At 50% sparsity, estimated total-memory reduction is 0% for both distilgpt2 and gpt2.
interpretation: The index metadata cancels out the value-memory savings.

finding: 75% sparsity gives similar total-memory savings to fp16 in this approximation.
evidence: Average 75% sparsity reduction is 46.29%, while average fp16 reduction is 46.29%.
interpretation: Sparse storage needs quite high sparsity to compete with simple dtype reduction.

finding: 90% sparsity gives strong memory reduction but still needs runtime validation.
interpretation: The analytical estimate is promising, but real sparse execution depends on kernels and hardware.

finding: Quantization is easier to reason about for memory than unstructured sparsity.
evidence: Quantization reduces bytes per value, while unstructured sparsity also adds index metadata.
interpretation: Sparsity has a more complicated memory tradeoff than dtype reduction.

finding: The sparsity phase is analytical, not measured runtime profiling.
evidence: No sparse CUDA kernels, sparse matrix multiplications, or compressed model execution were measured.
interpretation: The project should clearly label sparsity results as analytical estimates.
